course.title: AP Precalculus
course.description: Build the function toolkit that calculus depends on: how quantities change together, polynomial and rational functions, exponential and logarithmic models, and trigonometric and polar functions.
course.previewDescription: Study how outputs change with inputs, then use polynomial, rational, exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric functions to describe patterns and build models.

unit.title: Trigonometric and Polar Functions
unit.description: Model periodic phenomena with sine, cosine, and tangent, use inverse trigonometric functions and identities, and describe how polar functions change.

topic.title: Trigonometric Equations and Inequalities
topic.summary: Solving equations and inequalities involving trigonometric functions: one solution from an inverse function, the others from symmetry and periodicity, and the domain restrictions that a context implies.

questions.prompt: What are all solutions of 2 cos θ + 1 = 0 on the interval 0 ≤ θ < 2π?
questions.explanation: cos θ = −1/2. arccos(−1/2) = 2π/3, and the second solution is 2π − 2π/3 = 4π/3.
choiceExplanations: arccos gives only 2π/3; cosine is also −1/2 in Quadrant III.
cos(π/3) = 1/2, which has the wrong sign.
Quadrants II and III, both related to π/3.
questions.distinguisher: The inverse gives one solution; look for the second in the same period.

questions.prompt: Which of the following gives all solutions of tan θ = 1? (k represents any integer.)
questions.explanation: arctan(1) = π/4, and tangent has period π, so every solution is π/4 + kπ.
choiceExplanations: Tangent repeats every π.
This misses 5π/4, −3π/4, and every other solution, because tangent's period is π, not 2π.
These are the solutions on 0 ≤ θ < 2π, not all solutions.
questions.distinguisher: Add multiples of tangent's period, π.

questions.prompt: How many solutions does sin θ = 0.8 have on the interval 0 ≤ θ < 4π?
questions.explanation: Each period of length 2π contains two solutions, one in Quadrant I and one in Quadrant II. The interval 0 ≤ θ < 4π contains two periods, so there are 4 solutions.
choiceExplanations: arcsin(0.8) gives one solution, but there are more.
There are 2 solutions in one period, and this interval has two periods.
2 per period, 2 periods.
8 counts too many: there are only two periods in [0, 4π).

questions.prompt: To the nearest thousandth, what are all solutions of cos θ = 0.3 on the interval 0 ≤ θ < 2π?
questions.explanation: arccos(0.3) ≈ 1.266. Cosine is also 0.3 in Quadrant IV, at 2π − 1.266 ≈ 5.017.
choiceExplanations: π − 1.266 ≈ 1.875 is the second-solution rule for sine; cos(1.875) ≈ −0.3.
The inverse gives one solution; there is another in Quadrant IV.
0.305 and 2.837 solve sin θ = 0.3.
arccos(0.3) and 2π − arccos(0.3).
questions.distinguisher: For cosine the second solution is 2π − θ₁, not π − θ₁.

questions.prompt: What is the solution of sin θ > 1/2 on the interval 0 ≤ θ < 2π?
questions.explanation: sin θ = 1/2 at π/6 and 5π/6, and the graph of y = sin θ is above y = 1/2 between them.
choiceExplanations: This is where sin θ < 1/2, the complement.
sin θ > 1/2 on a wider interval; at π/4, sin θ ≈ 0.71 > 1/2.
Between the two solutions of sin θ = 1/2.
At θ = π, sin θ = 0, which is not greater than 1/2.
questions.distinguisher: Check one test point between the solutions.

questions.prompt: What is the solution of cos θ ≤ 0 on the interval 0 ≤ θ < 2π?
questions.explanation: cos θ = 0 at π/2 and 3π/2, and cos θ < 0 between them, in Quadrants II and III. The inequality includes equality, so the endpoints are included.
choiceExplanations: The inequality is ≤, so the zeros π/2 and 3π/2 are included.
cos θ > 0 for 0 ≤ θ < π/2.
cos θ > 0 for 3π/2 < θ < 2π.
The x-coordinate of P is not positive in Quadrants II and III and on the y-axis.

questions.prompt: A Ferris wheel rider's height is h(t) = 25 − 20 cos((π/4)t) meters, t minutes after boarding, for one ride, 0 ≤ t ≤ 8. For which values of t is the rider more than 35 meters above the ground?
choiceExplanations: This solves cos((π/4)t) > 1/2, which ignores the negative sign in front of 20.
2 < t < 6 is where the rider is above the midline, 25 meters.
4/3 < t < 20/3 is where the rider is above 15 meters.
questions.distinguisher: Isolate the cosine carefully: dividing by −20 reverses the inequality.

questions.prompt: The angle θ, in radians, between a ladder and the ground satisfies sin θ = 0.6. In this context, how many solutions does the equation have, and what are they?
choices: No solutions, because 0.6 is not an exact value
questions.explanation: A ladder leaning on the ground makes an angle 0 < θ < π/2 with it. Only one solution lies in that interval: θ = arcsin(0.6) ≈ 0.644.
choiceExplanations: 2.498 is more than π/2, which a ladder resting on the ground cannot make.
The context implies 0 < θ < π/2, which keeps one solution.
Adding full revolutions does not describe a real ladder angle.
arcsin(0.6) is a real number even though it is not one of the special angles.
questions.distinguisher: The context restricts the domain before you count solutions.

questions.prompt: What are all solutions of sin(2θ) = 0 on the interval 0 ≤ θ < 2π?
choices: θ = 0, θ = π/2, θ = π, and θ = 3π/2
questions.explanation: sin(2θ) = 0 when 2θ = kπ, so θ = kπ/2. On 0 ≤ θ < 2π that gives 0, π/2, π, and 3π/2.
choiceExplanations: These solve sin θ = 0. With 2θ, the solutions are twice as close together.
At θ = π/4, sin(2θ) = sin(π/2) = 1.
2π is not in the interval, and π/2 and 3π/2 are missing.
questions.distinguisher: Solve for 2θ first, then divide by 2.

questions.prompt: To solve sin θ = −1/2 on 0 ≤ θ < 2π, a student finds arcsin(−1/2) = −π/6 and says the only solution is θ = −π/6. Which of the following is the best response?
choices: The student is correct, because arcsine gives the solution.
The student is incorrect, because the solutions are θ = 7π/6 and θ = 11π/6.
The student is incorrect, because the solutions are θ = 5π/6 and θ = 7π/6.
The student is incorrect, because the solutions are θ = π/6 and θ = 5π/6.
questions.explanation: −π/6 is outside 0 ≤ θ < 2π, so it must be modified: −π/6 + 2π = 11π/6. The other solution is π − (−π/6) = 7π/6.
choiceExplanations: −π/6 is not in the interval 0 ≤ θ < 2π, and sine takes the value −1/2 twice per period.
These solve sin θ = 1/2.
questions.distinguisher: Move the inverse's answer into the interval, then find the second solution.
